g_1406645de654:
Lifecycle of the master key.
*
All user data is encrypted with a single AES-GCM-256 master key. This
module decides how that key is protected at rest, and nothing else.
*
One structural decision: **the master key is never extractable**. The
browser handles it without ever letting JavaScript read its bytes. The
price is explicit — it cannot be re-wrapped to move from one protection
mode to another. Changing protection will therefore mean generating a new
key and re-encrypting the data (phase 4). That is not a workaround:
rotating the key when protection changes is exactly what we want, since
the old key disappears with it.
*
What "device" mode protects, and what it does not:
  ✔ a raw copy of the profile or the disk — the records are unusable
    without the key, which exists nowhere in readable form;
  ✘ someone who launches *your* browser with *your* session — they get
    the same key you do. Only a passphrase answers that threat.
The interface must say both, without rounding off.

g_181c7ef837ee:
The vault — the only API the interface consumes.
*
Everything underneath (IndexedDB, AES-GCM, the tree, the migrations) is a
detail `src/ui` is not allowed to know. A test enforces it: see
`core/architecture.test.ts`.
*
Two guarantees are kept here, and nowhere else:
*
1. **The index and the documents never diverge.** Every mutation encrypts
   what it must write, *then* writes the document and the index in a
   single transaction. A crash at the wrong moment leaves the previous
   state, never an index referencing a missing document.
*
2. **The index lives in memory, decrypted once.** The sidebar, the command
   palette and the breadcrumbs therefore never have to decrypt a document
   in order to render.

g_27f0062332c7:
A view over an ordinary `ArrayBuffer`.
*
`Uint8Array` has been generic over its buffer since TypeScript 5.7, in
order to distinguish memory shared between threads (`SharedArrayBuffer`) —
which WebCrypto refuses. The alias avoids repeating that on every
signature, and makes any attempt to encrypt a shared buffer fail to
compile.
